{{Short description|Type of complex function with growth bounded by an exponential function}}
{{for|exponential types in type theory and programming languages|Function type}}
[[File:ExtremeGaussian.png|thumb|The graph of the function in gray is <math>e^{-\pi z^{2}}</math>, the Gaussian restricted to the real axis. The Gaussian does not have exponential type, but the functions in red and blue are one sided approximations that have exponential type <math>2\pi</math>.]]

In [[complex analysis]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a [[holomorphic function]] is said to be of '''exponential type C''' if its [[bounded growth|growth is bounded]] by the [[exponential function]] <math>e^{C|z|}</math> for some [[real number|real-valued]] constant <math>C</math> as <math>|z|\to\infty</math>.  When a function is bounded in this way, it is then possible to express it as certain kinds of convergent summations over a series of other complex functions, as well as understanding when it is possible to apply techniques such as [[Borel summation]], or, for example, to apply the [[Mellin transform]], or to perform approximations using the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula]]. The general case is handled by [[Nachbin's theorem]], which defines the analogous notion of '''<math>\Psi</math>-type''' for a general function <math>\Psi(z)</math> as opposed to <math>e^z</math>.

==Basic idea==

A function <math>f(z)</math> defined on the [[complex plane]] is said to be of exponential type if there exist real-valued constants <math>M</math> and <math>\tau</math> such that

:<math>\left|f\left(re^{i\theta}\right)\right| \le Me^{\tau r}</math>

in the limit of <math>r\to\infty</math>. Here, the [[complex variable]] <math>z</math> was written as <math>z=re^{i\theta}</math> to emphasize that the limit must hold in all directions <math>\theta</math>. Letting <math>\tau</math> stand for the [[infimum]] of all such <math>\tau</math>, one then says that the function <math>f</math> is of ''exponential type <math>\tau</math>''.

For example, let <math>f(z)=\sin(\pi z)</math>. Then one says that <math>\sin(\pi z)</math> is of exponential type <math>\pi</math>, since <math>\pi</math> is the smallest number that bounds the growth of <math>\sin(\pi z)</math> along the imaginary axis. So, for this example, [[Carlson's theorem]] cannot apply, as it requires functions of exponential type less than <math>\pi</math>. Similarly, the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula]] cannot be applied either, as it, too, expresses a theorem ultimately anchored in the theory of [[finite difference]]s.

==Formal definition==
A [[holomorphic function]] <math>F(z)</math> is said to be of '''exponential type''' <math>\sigma>0</math> if for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there exists a real-valued constant <math>A_\varepsilon </math> such that

:<math>|F(z)|\leq A_\varepsilon e^{(\sigma+\varepsilon)|z|}</math>

for <math>|z|\to\infty</math> where <math>z\in\mathbb{C}</math>.
We say <math>F(z)</math> is of exponential type if <math>F(z)</math> is of exponential type <math>\sigma</math> for some <math>\sigma>0</math>. The number

:<math>\tau(F)=\sigma=\displaystyle\limsup_{|z|\rightarrow\infty}|z|^{-1}\log|F(z)|</math>
[[File:Example exponential type 1 function.png|thumb|500px|Behavior of <math>F(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{z^{10^{n!}}}{(10^{n!})!}.</math> The ratio of <math>\log|F(z)|</math> to <math>|z|</math> at a given radius is maximized on the real axis.]]
is the exponential type of <math>F(z)</math>. The [[limit superior]] here means the limit of the [[supremum]] of the ratio outside a given radius as the radius goes to infinity. This is also the limit superior of the maximum of the ratio at a given radius as the radius goes to infinity. The limit superior may exist even if the maximum at radius <math>r</math> does not have a limit as <math>r</math> goes to infinity. For example, for the function

:<math>F(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{z^{10^{n!}}}{(10^{n!})!}</math>

the value of

:<math> (\max_{|z|=r} \log|F(z)|) / r</math>

at <math>r=10^{n!-1}</math> is dominated by the {{mvar|n}}−1{{sup|st}} term and this goes to zero as <math>n</math> goes to infinity,<ref>In fact, even <math>(\max_{|z|=r}\log \log|F(z)|) /(\log r)</math> at <math>r=10^{n!-1}</math> goes to zero as 
<math>n</math> goes to infinity.</ref> but <math>F(z)</math> is nevertheless of exponential type 1, as can be seen by looking at the points <math>z=10^{n!}</math>.

==Exponential type with respect to a symmetric convex body==

{{harvtxt|Stein|1957}} has given a generalization of exponential type for [[entire function]]s of [[several complex variables]]. 
Suppose <math>K</math> is a [[convex set|convex]], [[compact element|compact]], and [[symmetric]] subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. It is known that for every such <math>K</math> there is an associated [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] <math>\|\cdot\|_K</math> with the property that

:<math> K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n : \|x\|_K \leq1\}. </math>

In other words, <math>K</math> is the unit ball in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> with respect to <math>\|\cdot\|_K</math>. The set

:<math>K^{*}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:x\cdot y \leq 1 \text{ for all }x\in{K}\}</math>

is called the [[polar set]] and is also a [[convex set|convex]], [[compact element|compact]], and [[symmetric]] subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. Furthermore, we can write

:<math>\|x\|_K = \displaystyle\sup_{y\in K^{*}}|x\cdot y|.</math>

We extend <math>\|\cdot\|_K</math> from <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> to <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math> by

:<math>\|z\|_K = \displaystyle\sup_{y\in K^{*}}|z\cdot y|.</math>

An entire function <math>F(z)</math> of <math>n</math>-complex variables is said to be of exponential type with respect to <math>K</math> if for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> there exists a real-valued constant <math>A_\varepsilon</math> such that

:<math>|F(z)|<A_\varepsilon e^{2\pi(1+\varepsilon)\|z\|_K}</math>

for all <math>z\in\mathbb{C}^{n}</math>.

==Fréchet space==
Collections of functions of exponential type <math>\tau</math> can form a [[complete space|complete]] [[uniform space]], namely a [[Fréchet space]], by the [[topological space|topology]] induced by the countable family of [[norm (mathematics)|norm]]s

: <math> \|f\|_n = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{C}} \exp \left[-\left(\tau + \frac{1}{n}\right)|z|\right]|f(z)|. </math>
